summary:
We built Stratanauts Space Mission, a free browser game that teaches space mission design
as one connected system instead of a set of separate subjects. A student picks a world
and a mission, then designs a spacecraft through fourteen decisions — route, objectives,
budget, fuel, power, communications, science instruments, vehicle — where every choice
spends from a single mass and delta-v budget. Before launch, seven mission stations
(booster, propulsion, power, communications, thermal, guidance and range safety) vote GO
or HOLD, and the space-weather station reads live NASA DONKI solar-flare data. The player
must then either fix the holds or accept the risk, fly the countdown and orbit insertion,
and face a debrief that scores the decisions actually made. It solves the challenge by
making the trade-off, not the formula, the thing you learn: students feel why a kilogram
given to power is a kilogram taken from science. Mission design is normally taught behind
software licences and expensive labs, so the students who most need systems thinking
never meet it. Stratanauts needs no install, no account and no payment, runs in any
modern browser, and ships in six languages (English, Bengali, Hindi, Spanish, Arabic,
French), so a classroom with one shared device can still run a full mission. It is an
independent educational project, not endorsed by NASA, released under the team's own licence.

Project Files=https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Jts2UfUQ1wBiBzPCA4undR-qZnh7Rxiu/view?usp=drive_link

pdf demonstration=https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ofS1Ew6V8WT0Zenqcsnv3BOK--5crkgO/preview

THE PROBLEM. Mission design is normally split across lessons: orbital mechanics here, propulsion there, budgets in a spreadsheet, operations in a textbook. Students memorise the formulas and never make a decision with a cost, so the central skill — trading mass, power, propellant and risk against each other under one constraint — stays abstract. The students who would benefit most are also the least likely to meet it: no simulator licence, no lab, often one shared device.

WHAT WE BUILT. A playable 3D mission hub and a fourteen-step mission-control flow. From the hub, the player opens Flight Plan and chooses a world (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter or Saturn), a mission type and a route; the destination fixes the constraints that follow. The fourteen steps walk objectives, budget, fuel, power, communications, science instruments and the spacecraft itself. Each screen shows what the choice costs in mass and delta-v out of one shared budget, with a 'Learn why' panel explaining the physics behind the number. In the hangar the player swaps engines (RL10 chemical, NSTAR ion, NERVA nuclear thermal), tanks, solar wings, an MMRTG power source, antennas and instruments, and watches mass, power and delta-v margin update live. Running the launch check calls a seven-station readiness poll — booster, propulsion, power, communications, thermal, guidance and range safety — where each station returns GO, HOLD or NO-GO based on the vehicle the player actually built, with the space-weather station reading live NASA DONKI solar-flare data. The player can go back and fix the holds, or explicitly accept the risk, then fly the countdown, ascent and injection burn, work the hazard decision on arrival and receive a Mission Report that scores what they did and generates lessons from their own choices. A separate Learn area adds a Science Lab (rocket equation, orbits, sunlight and signal delay) with a narrated mentor, seven interactive steps per topic.

HOW IT USES NASA DATA. Live at run time: NASA APOD, NASA NeoWs, NASA DONKI (solar flares), the NASA Image and Video Library and JPL Horizons. Reference values behind the model come from NSSDCA planetary fact sheets and published NASA figures for SLS/Orion, the RL10 upper-stage engine, the NSTAR ion thruster, NERVA and the MMRTG. When a NASA endpoint is unreachable the app falls back to bundled snapshots and labels the provenance on screen as DEMO DATA rather than pretending the number is live.

VALIDITY. The budget arithmetic is deterministic and unit-checked, and every constant is cited in the documentation, so the same mission replays to the same numbers. The debrief is derived from the player's own decisions, not from a random roll.

ACCESSIBILITY AND REACH. Free, no account, no install, no tracking; a modern browser on desktop or mobile; interface and content in six languages. Released under the team's own licence, free for education, so a school can fork it and build a local curriculum around it.

WHAT IS NEXT. Teacher mode with class codes and printable debriefs, exportable mission logs so a teacher can assess the decision trace rather than a final score, more worlds and vehicles, and reviewed translations with regional classrooms.

Contribute and made by Team The Stratanauts, six members, Kopargaon, India: Rehan Shaikh, Shubham Tanpure, Atharav Joshi, Tejas Thombare, Omkar Karad and Tejas Dhavane.

Independent educational project. Not endorsed by NASA. AI (SI) assistance is declared in the Use of SI answer and in AI-Use-Disclosure.pdf.
